code.highlightReason: @Valid tells Spring MVC to validate the deserialised request DTO before the controller method runs.
code.intro: Validation is not automatic merely because a DTO has constraints.
code.takeaway: Put constraints on request DTOs and add @Valid at the HTTP boundary; invalid input should not reach service code.
code.title: Bean Validation starts at @Valid

hook.headline: Constraints alone do nothing.
hook.hook: Spring only runs request validation when the controller asks it to.
hook.visualCaption: Validate untrusted HTTP input before business logic.

interview.answer: Bean Validation constraints on a request DTO are metadata until Spring MVC is asked to apply them. Adding @Valid to an @RequestBody parameter validates the deserialised object before the controller body executes. Invalid input normally becomes a 400 response, which can be standardised with exception handling.
interview.question: Why can a Spring controller accept an invalid DTO even when its fields have @NotBlank or @Email?

mentalModel.coreIdea: A request DTO is populated first; validation is a separate, explicit step at the MVC boundary.

problems: Forgetting @Valid silently lets bad data enter service and persistence layers.
Nested DTOs need @Valid on the nested field for cascaded validation.
production.professionalApproach: Validate transport-level shape and basic invariants at the API boundary; keep cross-record and business-state rules in the service layer.
